We learn that the North of England Arbitration

The miners in the Oldham district a fortnight
ago sent in a request for a further advance of 15
per cent. A meeting of delegates was held in
the Temperance Hall on Wednesday night, and
they reported that the advance would be granted.

THE POSTAL AND TELEGRAPH

SERVICE.

THE EDINBURGH LEITER CARRIERS.

On the 12th ult. the letter carriers of Edinburgh
and Leith presented a petition to the Postmaster-
General, together with a letter to the Secretary,
soliciting an improvement in their position, and
the following answer has been received. It is
addressed to the bead inspector, and is as follows:
—" Mr. Simpson,—l have been authorized by
Mr. Cunyngham to instruct you to inform the
letter carriers that the Postmaster-General has
again carefully examined the mutter of their
memorial, but he is unable to propose to the
Lords of the Treasury that any further change
should be made in their scale of wages recently
sanctioned. Mr. Monsell presumes that it cannot
be contended that the cost of living is any greater
at Edinburgh than at Liverpool or Manchester,
and therefore it does not appear that an exception
should be made in the case of Edinburgh. lam
directed further to notice that the letter carriers
also arsk for a reduction of their hours of labour,
suggesting that with this object the two evening
deliveries should be amalgamated, and that instead
of half, they may be altuwed twoghirds of their
wages when absent from illness. The amalgama-
tion of the two deliveries is a matter in regard to
which it is not the place of the letter carriers to
suggest what should be the policy of the depart-
ment as regards postal arrangements; and with
respect to the allowance during absence from ill-
ness, the letter carriers are informed that the re-
gulation in the benefit of which they share is of
general application save as reg (Hs a few officers
where a special regulation previously existed.
That they are mistaken in supposing that a higher
rate of allowance than 'the rate they enjoy has
recently been granted to the Birmingham letter
carriers. 'Under these circumstances the .Post-
master-General is not prepared ti make fresh ex-
ceptions, or any general alteration in the rate.—
Signed, W. J. Seville, superintendent, Sept. 30th,
1872."

A most decisive answer that certainly, 1
and a snubbing one too, and savours much of
coming from a lower order than that of the Post-
master-General. The employes say we here, at
least, give the Postrue,ater-General credit for •..a
higher standard of gentlemanly manners than to
condescend to issue such an answer to a respect-
ful petition presented to him by a respectable body
of men: This last piece may not sound well in
coining from us, but it is well-known that if we
were not respectable we would not occupy the
position which we at present do. We therefore
consider the matter of the answer to our petition
to be much more out of place than our suggest-
ing to the authorities that our labour should be
reduced by the amalgamation or the two evening
deliveries. As we nlrealy said we consider the
above answer in toto never came from, or at least
never was the work of the Postmaster-General.
If it did emanate from him, we can only say it
has lowered him considerably in our estimation.
There is much in it, however, to assure us that he
is no psrty thereto, as, for instance, it seems but
now that he has learned that "it is not the place
of the letter carriers to suggest what should be
the policy of the department in regard to postal
arrangements." Be it understood that in our
former petition there was a sentence similar to the
one complained of, and the answer thereto was so
far satisfactory, being to the effect "that the
authorities could not see their way to make such
an arrangement at present." This was else a re-
fusal to grant what we desired, but then it was a
polite one, and as such was received by Us in a
quiet manner. The answer this time, however,
has opened up a very great question, viz., have
we, or have we not, a right to inuke suggestions
regsrding our work, the carrying out of which
would benefit the public and ourselves? We an-
swer in the affirmative ; the postal authorities in
the negative,

As the subject is one of too groat import-

anoe to be quickly disposed of, we will,
with your leave, defer the discussion till another
time. Before concluding we desire to say a word
or two relative to the last clause of the answer to
our memorial, viz., "that we are mistaken in sup-
posing that a higher rate of sickness allowance'
than the rate we enjoy has recently been granted
to the Birmingham letter carriers." Need we say

MR. ALEXANDER M‘DONALD ,

President of Minere' National Association, and

FOR more than a Quarter of a Century—
eighteen years incessantly has Mr.
lit Donald laboured to get the Miners of the

following their hazardous occupation shorter
hours of labour and education for the young—just
contracts of services; in short to enumerate all
the provisions would be out of place here—they
are besides, so well-kaown to all that they do not
need to be mentioned.
Suffice it to say that nearly every one of the
provisions he has so long claimed as the Miners'
right have now been incorporated in the Mines
Act of 1872, and already have great changes been
effected in the condition of the mining population
through his labours, but these will be still greater
'when the new Act comes into operation.

It is not too much to say that in the long years
of toil, almost without hope, Mr. M`Dunald has
made many sacrifices to health and comfort that
he /night have otherwise obtained. At the con.
elusion of the work so groat, we deem this a fit
and proper time to tender to him some substantial
recognition of his many services to the cause of
the Miner, and in general to the cause of human
progress. To the Miners we would say show
your gratitude by your works in aid of the
Testimonial—let it be worthy of the man. To
others we say help.
I am, yours respectfully,

SATURDAY, OCTOBER 12, 1872.

EARL FORTESCUE ON CLASS
EDUCATION.
WE have no doubt of the existence of such
a being as the true gentleman. There are men
who, rather than say or do an unworthy
thing, would pluck out their own tongue or
chop off their right hand. Such, no doubt,
are to be found in every class of human
society, beginning with kings and ending
with beggars. With these convictions, we
are more than ready to believe that the Earl
FORTES= did not mean to injure or misre-
present any body in his speech at Sainpford
reverill, a village in Devonshire. Anti yet
he did not succeed altogether, unless the
papers have misreported him, in avoiding
a matter which must challenge criticism. As
he was presiding at the yearly meeting of a
middle-class school belonging to the county,
it was but natural for him to touch upon any
topic connected with the instruction of boys
whose parents are of that class.
The noble EARL began by lamenting the want
of training among middle-class school teachers.
This, we believe, is an old defect, and very
generally acknowledged. An old :defect, as
shown, not simply by prevalent mediocrity of
talent and attainment among the sellout-
masters and their assistants, but by the
apparent indifference of generations of parent

to the style and character of the education, so
called, given to their sons. Middle-class
schools have long had the bad repute of paying
chief attention to what is purely mechanical
and imitative, such as handwriting, and of
neglecting, or. mis-teaching, things most
essential to the disciplining of the mental
faculties, and to the preparing of the boy to
store his mind, in Youth and manhood, with
a well-acquired and a well-ordered store of
really necessary and useful knowledge.
We had thought, however, that the College
of Preceptors, and some other measures pro-
moted by the better sort of middle-class school-
masters, were doing, and indeed had already
done, a good deal towards, a general and an
effective reform. Somewhere, nevertheless,
Lord FORTESCUE has picked up the notion,
that the number of teachers both for and from
the middle-class is decreasing. We arc at a
loss to know on what data he grounds such a
conclusion. There is no doubt, indeed, that
the designation " middle-class" covers an
immense space, and comprises, not merely a
great many people, but also a variety equally
as great. The term, in fact, is too vague and
indefinite for Such strictures as those of Lord
FORTESCITE to be founded upon it; for it is
used to deScribe quite a mixture of persons,
beginning with such as arc, in no social sense,
to be discriminated from mechanics and
artisans, and terminating with the learned
professions, bankers, merchants, and manu-
facturers, whom, some on account of wealth,
and others on account of manners and culture,
it is hardly possible to distinguish from "the
lords of the soil," except to the disadvantage
of the less cultivated among the latter.

articles.title: Only a full and carefully collected know-
articles.text:
Only a full and carefully collected know-

ledge of facts would justify a strong assertion on
the subject; but there are indications on the
surface which scarcely support Lord FOR-
TESCITE'S impression of a dearth of middle-
class teachers of middle-class youths. To
name but one, the half-yearly flood of
boarding-school advertisements which inun-
dates newspaper columns and magazine
covers, rises higher and higher, instead of
falling lower and lower, on each recurrence.
This, however, by the bye. What we must
more decidedly take exception to in the noble
EMIL'S observations is the tendency they seem
to us to have, though we sincerely acquit
him of so designing, to minister to jealous
feeling on the part of the middle-class in
respect of instructed men emerging from the
working class. Most of the teachers for the
middle-class, he thinks, do not come from that
class. That may be, though we greatly doubt
it. A great many of the boarding-schools are
kept by clergymen of the Church of England,
a considerable number by graduates of the old
Universities or of the University of London;
and, in a large portion of the remainder,
where the principals are not graduates, their
senior assistants are. Generally speaking, the
proprietors.of boarding-schools are undoubtedly
men of the middle-class. It was lately ques-
tioned whether farm-labourers ever rise to be
master-farmers, and. the doubt has been con-
futed by the production of instances. We
believe it might much more safely be ques-
tioned whether there are among boarding-
school keepers men who belonged originally to
the working class, though we should not be
surprised to hear of such examples, because
already fully persuaded that many of the best
in the usher grade are meritorious young men,
who by talent, industry, and good character
have reached that modest position from be-
ginnings so humble as to make it seem to
them a proud one.
Lord FORTESCUE thinks there must be
something unsound and unsatisfactory in the
training of the middle-class, and the for-
mation of their character being carried on
almost exclusively by those who sprang from
another class, If this reasoning be sound,
must there not be something equally unsound
and unsatisfaotory in the training of the
upper elass, for precisely the same reason?
Perhaps his lordship admits all graduates of
Oxford and Cambridge within the pale of his
own class, espeohilly if they are clergy men-
It is certain, at any rate, that not simply
squires and nobles, but even Princes of the
Blood, are indebted for their education to such
graduates, men who, if, as graduates admitted

among the upper class, " sprang" at least
from another class, We emphasise this appli-
cation of the noble EARL'S objection, because,
in a moment or two, we shall have occasion to
recur to it. When, indeed, he warns the
middle class of the possible effect to them-
selves of their falling, in point of knowledge
and instruction, " behind those whom they
are to employ and direct," nobody has
any right to complain. Least of all
have working men, who, we believe, will
always have most confidence in employers
who are themselves educated men, and also
the best reason for entertainining such
confidence. But, when this Southern Peer
makes it a "matter of groat importance that
the teaching of the middle class should not
be in the hands of those who sympathise with
the wage-receiving instead of with the wage-
paying class," he gives expression to a senti-
ment which we should take the liberty of con-
demning as illiberal, divisive, and unjust,
were we quite sure that the words as delivered
were unaccompanied by other words, before or
after, adapted to take off an appearance so
repulsive and regrehonsible.
Surely Lord FORTESCUE cannot have gone

through the courae of his own school inetruo-
tion and University training without having
acquired a better knowledge of facts than the
words imputed to him seem to imply. In
the first place, there is no class of teachers
better trained, so far as they go, than the
worthy men who hold first-rate certificates
under the Committee of Council on Education;

and, in the second place, though our informa-
tion on this point is less exact, we believe that
to be an acknowledged member of the College
of Preceptors is an equally satisfactory testi-
mony to a man's fitness in all respects to he
a master or teacher in any middle-class
boarding or day school. But, were we asked
to name the most signal instance in which the
men of one class have been indebted for their
instruction to men sprung from another clasq,
we should without hesitation take the taught
from the highest class of all, and the teachers
from what is deemed by some people the

lowest class of all. The sons of peasants have
over and over again filled the highest plaoes in
schools, colleges, and the Church. The most

erudite scholar and deepest philosopher of our
own times, a mail who lived and died. a
teacher, was the son of a working carpenter
in the country; and it is the commonest of all
occurrences in Oxford and Cambridge to find
incurable laziness, unteaohable blookheadism,
and depraved morals among the sons of noble-
men and squires; while, at both Universities,
the rarer ranks of reading men, and of those
who read to most purpose, whether for solid
knowledge or for fleeting honours, are often
replenished and constantly illustrated from the
sons of working men, farmers, and small
tradesmen, who, by dint of talent and in-
dustry, sometimes aided by generous sym-
pathy, have worked their way up from the
foot of the ladder of learning up to its highest
round.

EMIGRATION AND PAUPERISM.

A PARAGRAPH a few days since went the
round of our newspapers, headed "Increase
in Emigration from Liverpool." Without
going into particulars, it may be stated that
the increase from Liverpool alone on the nine
months of the present year over the same
period of last year is no less than 21,001 per-
sons. The English contingent for the last
three months being no fewer than 19,000.

Why is it that the working people of Eng-
land are thus flying from the land of their
birth as though it was plague-stricken ? With
all our prosperity of trade—with our great
increase of wealth—notwithstanding the many
songs of triumph we are singing to signalise
our wonderful progress as a nation, the masses
of our people seem to have found out that
England is no safe home for them, and
struggle to get away as fast as their limited
means will permit. In fifteen years this out-
flow has about doubled itself, and all the time
the wealth of England has been increasing.
The prosperous year 1871 gives us an emigra-
tion return of 232,435, and these for the most
part English people, who are carried oft' by
, the ()allowing stream almost as rapidly as the
1 people of Trelargl, were during the faMin°

exodus. We have seen no analysis distin-
guishing between the mere labourers and the
skilled artizans, but there can be little doubt
that every kind of skilled occupation con-
tributes its quota, and that the United States
of America, to which this mighty tlaod is
directed, is thus possessing itself of a trained
population which will 'contribute more than
anything else to its future mastery as a great
manufacturing and commercial country. Bell-
gious persecutions in France gave us a silk
trade ; an immigration from the low countries
gave us mastery in woollen manufactures, but
these lucky additions to our manufacturing
population were the merest trifles compared
to the crowds we are now sending to strengthen
the hands of the most powerful and enter-
prising rival we have got in the various fields
of productive industry.
This may ultimately turn out to be the very
best thing for the world that could have hap-
pened. At the same time it may be the very
worst thing for England as a nation. Whatever
comes of it, with us it is a matter of necessity,
not of choice. We cannot find profitable
constant employment for our people, and
hence we cannot prevent them either from
leaving us, or from swelling that huge welter-
ing mass of pauperism which, except for
short exceptional periods, grows year by year
to a foul and most dangerous increase. The
Government returns in regard to our poor and
poor-rates are absolutely frightful. The last
"Statistical Abstract" published, which gives
the figures from 1857 to 1871, is most dis-
couraging. The amount at the first period
expended in actual relief of the poor was
£5,898,756; whilst in the latter year it was
£7,886,724. This difference it may be noted
was in no way due to exceptional causes, but
was the result of a gradual, regular increase,
entirely due to causes constantly active as Part
of our social and political system.
It is right to add here, that besides this
alarming sum for pauperism, there is collected
with it county and police rates, which intimate
the cost to the nation of our criminal classes,
and these, as may naturally be expected, have
had a corresponding development. In 1867
hey amounted to £,440,454; but in 1871
:hey had risen to the stun of ,D 1,206,017.

It will thus be seen that we have in
England, as it were, two nations, or two
great, widely contrasting divisions of the
same nation, separated by a gulf which
becomes every day wider and deeper, and
across which many angry scowls are oast,
and loud threats and complaints uttered, as
from enemies who may some day have to
prepare themselves for deadly conflict.
The prosperous become every day more
prosperous—the wretched more miserable and
unhappy; whilst our Government, hopeless
of being able to reconcile contending interests,
or in any way to strike at the root of these
our worst evils, looks helplessly on at our
daily depletion by emigration, and at our
dangerously increasing tumour of pauperism.
No treatment is suggested for the first; the
second receives the mild palliative handling
of an incurable malady. The Whigs look at
it and shake their heads; the Tories glance at
it and sigh—over everything else those parties
differ and fight. In regard to this the Whig
and the Tory are as much alike as one rotten
egg is like another ; and equally helpless in
grappling with these worst evils of the nation.
The working men, who in this bad business
are the principal sufferers, may find out a
remedy, or may insist on some sort of decided
effort being made by those who claim and
hold a monopoly of government to attempt
a remedy. At present, however, there is not
any very encouraging sign that anything of
this sort will take place. Our rival administra-
tions trust to the old treatment; new candi-
dates for Parliamentary honours have nothing
to say to the matter; whilst the working men
as a rule are, either Liberals or Conservatives
In the old sense, the dopes and the tools too
frequently at the right moment of those jaunty
gentlemen known as electioneering agents.

and that the cost and loss entails a burden
under the present system of £177,630,970, in
addition to the net revenue—how can they (the
landowners) base infatuated as to tolerate so
suicidal a policy.?
"So intimately connected are the interests
of trade and agriculture, that they may be
taken as concurrent; for all experience shows
that a state of prosperity or depression in the
one is the same in the other, It, therefore,
can need no words to prove that, by relieving
trade from all taxes or other impositions or
impediments, no injury can thereby be in-

CO-OPERA.TI VE MINIM ACT URING.

On Saturday a large conference of represen-
tatives from co-operative souieties in all parts
of Yorkshire, together with delegates from the
Wholesale Society, in Manchester, and from
other towns in England and Scotland, was
held in the Halifax Industrial Society's stores;
Mr. J. 'Whiteley presiding. The Conferenee
was called by the Caldeidale, Airedale, and
Dewsbury districts' and there were eighty
societies represented. The districts first-of all
resolved to form themselves into an organiza-
tion to .be known as the Yorkshire Union of Co-
operative Societies, after which the question
was introduced, by Mr. Nuttall, of Oldham, of
forming a society for the manufacture of
flannels and blankets. There arc allready
several mills existing in Yorkshire conducted
partly on the co-operative system, and it was
urged that if a manufactory was started upon
purely co-operative principles by a federation
of the societies, and under the auspices of the
Wholesale Society, a large business would be
done amongst • the stores which would share
the profits. 111 r.. N-uttall reeved, " That the
Wholesale Society be recommended to enter
into the production of blankets and flannels in
conjunotien with a local board, selected by
local stores, and that the Wholesale Society be
also recommended to increase the number of its
directors, to enable them adequately to under-
take the management of the increased business
which would thus devolve upon them." As
an amendment, it Was moved, " That this
meeting recommends the. committee of the
Yorkshire Union .of Co-operative Societies to
take into consideration the establishment of a
flannel and blanket manufactory, or the pur-
chasing .of one or more of those already, started,
and that it be supported by federated societies."
The amendment was passed.; upon which
further amendment was moved, to the effect
that the question be deferred until the quarterly
conference, to be held at Heckrnondwike, in
order to give the various Societies an oppor-
tunity of considering the best mode of action.
This amendment was agreed to, ani the eon-
ferenoe then concluded.

articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

The Queen and Princess Beatrice remained
at the Massalt Stile' on Sunday. Her
Majesty will probably hold a -council at
Balmoral on Tuesday next.

Mr. Justice Willes was buried at Ilrompton
Cemetery on Monday. The funeral was of a
private character.

The Archbishop of Ginterbury resumed his
visitation at St. Mary's, Ashford, on Monday,
and delivered a further portion of his charge.
One of the subjects he dealt with was
ecclesiastical legislation. He held that it was
not desirable that great ohanges should be
continually going on in the Church, but the
changing circumstances of the community
necessitated certain changes from time to
time, and the Church of England had shown
no inability to make such changes when they
were required. He also adverted to the
Athanasian Creed, and said he favoured the
removal of the Creed from the service, and its
adoption among the Articles, This was a most
difficult and intricate question, and he strongly
deprecated the conduct of those who, in dis-
cussing the Subject, declared that they would
breakup the Church, if it were proposed to
settle it in away which did not exactly agree
with their views.

Archbishop Manning has prohibited the
employment of female vocalists in the Roman
Catholic places of worship within his diocese.

Mr. Charles Mathews appeared at the
Gaiety Theatre on Tuesday night, after an
absence from this country of two years and
nine months, and was enthusiastically re-
ceived. Mr. Mathews took his old characters
of Sir Fretful Plagiary. and Puff in Sheridan's
Untie.

The trade and navigation returns for Sep,
tember have been *med. The aggregate
imports for the nine months of this year were
£261,310,336 being an increase of nearly
twenty millions over those of last year. The
exports for the same period were £190,314,662,
as again.st L 165,677,979 last year.

At the meeting of the Bermondsey Vestry
the other night a. letter was received from the
Bermondsey aud Rotherhithe blaster Bakers'
Association, requesting the vestry to carry out
the provisions, of the Food Adulteration Act,
so as to prevent the adulteration of bread. The
letter, it is stated, was received with laughter.

Cholera is announced to have made its
appearance on the Aland Islands, better
known to English readers through one of ,their
fortified ports—Sir Charles Napier's Bonier-
mud. On the adjoining coasts of Sweden and
Norway quarantine regulations have been

Two explosions of tire-damp ()warred on
Monday at the Mosley Main Colliery, between
Leeds and Dewsbury, and it is reported that
four lives have perished.

The punishment of flogging was adminis-
tered at Newgate on Monday on two prisoners,
George Cohen' a Jew, and William Johnson,
both of whom had been convicted of personal
robbery with violence.

Murphy, the victim of the supposed Fenian
outrage at Dublin on Friday, La, it is stated,
progressing favourably.

The October Sessions for the county of
Middlesex commenced on Monday, the previous
Sessions having closed only on Friday. There
was but a light calendar.

William Slater, a shipwright, was sentenced
to six months' imprisonment and hard labour
at the Thames Police-court on Monday for a
brutal assault on his with; and William Kettle,
another wife beater, was sentenced at Bow-
street Police-court to four months' imprison-

Whitbread's brewery, was brought up at the
Guildhall oh Monday charged with cutting hie
wile's throat. She wai tmable to attend, and

land is likely to be signed before the me,utiog

The ease of Mr. Frederick Strange, -Pro•

ments within the prohibited hours on Sunday
to persons not being bona fide travellers.

Walter James Cochrane, a boy of fifteen,
was committed for trial at the biarylebone
Police-court on Tuesday on a charge of cutting
and wounding another boy named Alfred'
Cooke.

Daring the week ending Saturday last,
2,188 births and 1,276 deaths were registered
in London, the births being 30 and the deaths
115 below the average numbers in the corres-
ponding week of the last ten years. The
1,276 deaths included 10 from small-pox, 9

mortality in London and twenty other large

to every 1,000 persons living, the rate in
London being 20 per 1,000; in Liverpool, 28;
in Manchester, 30; and in Oldham, where'
scarlet fever prevails, as high as 48.

On Tuesday afternoon a deputation of
artisans and working men presented the Lord
Mayor with a handsome glass claret jug, in
recognition of his efforts to secure Alexandra.
park for the use of the people.

The Church Congress opened at Leeds CU
Tuesday with a grand procession of bishops,:
Clergy, and laity from the Town-hall to the
Old Church. The sermon was preached by
the Archbishop of Armagh. The members
afterwards assembled at the Town-hall, where
the Bishop of Ripm delivered an inaugural;
address. A discussion followed upon ;he

The interment of Dr. Goss, late nomati
Catholio Bishop at Liverpool, took plttce at
Ford Cemetery, near that town, on Tuesdqs•
in the presence of large crowds of persons._ A:
solemn requiem mass was celebrated at CO.
peras-hill Chapel; after which Archbishop
Manning delivered au eloquent eulogium on
the deceased. It is stated that nearly 50,000
people were present at the cemetery.

Salvanos was the winner of the Cesarewiteh
Stakes at Newmarket on Tuesday. SAY&
came in second, and Enfield third.

being an increase of £2,253,673 over the
corresponding period of lost year. The ex 4
penditure was £38,717,322, and the balances
on the sth of October were in the Bank of
England, £1,618,633, and in the Bunk of

The itnportation of cattle into Denmark,
from Great Britain is prohibited, iu ono-,

A meeting was held in the Free Trade Hall,
Manchester, on Tuesday night, in support of
the disestablishment and diseudown3ent of the
Church of England. Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P.,
who presided, said a State Church could only
be maintained by violating the plainest
principles of justice. The State ought only to
support such institutions as received the com-
mon consent.

The number of Alsace and Lorraine inhabi-
tants who registered their names with the
German authorities as choosing French na-
tionality is 164,633. Of this number 38,000
really emigrated, thus making their option
Valid, and besides about 12,000 Frenchmen
domiciled in these parts have left since the 2nd
March, 1871.

At a meeting of the Town Council of Hamil-
ton it has been unanimously agreed to present
Mr. H. M. Stanley, the disooverer of Dr.
Livingstone, with the freedom of the burgh
on the occasion of his visit to Hamilton in
November.

Placards warning the public against ap-
proaching the red deer during the present
month of October have been affixed to some of
the trees standing in the Great Park, Windsor.
At this season of the year the red deer become
extremely fierce, audit is dangerous to go too
close to them.

King Amadeo has been the object of a new
attack. Two men concealed behind the statues
of the Place d'Orieut, situated in front of the
Royal Palace, threw at the king a large piece
of stone, with the intention of killing him.
The missile fell at the king's feet, and those
who had thrown it ran away. A sergeant of
the police ran after them, but was unable to
catch them. When throwing the stone the
authors of thii attempt uttered the cry of
Viva la Republique!

A warrant has been issued for the appre-
hension of Assistant-Paymaster Moses Pierov,
of her Majesty's ship 'GILT°, who absconded
from that ship at Portsmuuth on Saturday,
being £2OO in default on the ship's wine
account, and .£BO belonging to widows of men
drowned, which had been subscribed by the
officers and crew, is also missing.

Two Marshals, McMahon and Canrobert ;
two Admirals, De la lionoiere and Ozanne;
with the Duo d'Aumale and General La..itrai-
rault, will compose the Supreme Council of
War which is to be entrusted with the organi-
zation and administration of the French Army.

Two and tbree-quarter millions sterling
were collected during the war by the German
Aid Societies for tending the sick and wounded.
After paying all expenses incurred, a surplus
of fifty thousand pounds remains. The so-
cieties have determined to retain their
organization, with a view to future military
contingencies.

Window and show-bill taxation has provoked
a drawn battle between the municipality and
the shopkeepers of Madrid. All who incurred
this slightly antiquated impost shut up their
shops when it came into operation. Thus
silently protesting, they intend to wait for its
repeal. So. far there have been no public
disturbances.

In inaugurating the winter session of the
Birmingham and Midland Institute, Canon
Kingsley spoke about the physieal degeneracy
of the Itnglish commons. He dates its com-
meneemeut from the period of the Napoleonic
wars, which killed off the flower of English
youth, and reversed the Darwinian law of
survival of the fittest.

Field-Marshal Sir George Pollock has had
only a brief term of the Confitableship of the
Tower, He died unexpectedly on Sunday
morning, at Walmer.

A riot took place at Cincinnati on Monday
night between a procession of Greeley Clubs
and a Negro Military Company. Five men
were shot, all of whom were whites. The
origin of the affray is not known. The negroes
had muskets and bayonets. A. few whites
used pibtols.

Of the herd of thirty-six cattle attacked by
pleuro-pneumouia on the estate of Lord North-
brook, near Winchester, twenty-one have been
slaughtered, and the remaining fifteen have
died.

On Tuesday at Epsom, about nine o'clock, it
was discovered that a woman named Eliza-
beth Marehant had cut her throat and that of
her child, a little girl, about three years of
age. The unfortunate woman, with her child,
applied for lodgings for the night at the
Queen's Head inn, and not rising at the
usual time, the servant was horrified on enter-
ing the room to find her sitting up in bed,
the blood pouring from her throat and the
child lain across her knees, its head nearly
severed from its body. It is very doubtful
whether she will recover. A new razor was
found on the bed, covered with blood. , .

Lieutenant Helms, R.N., suddenly dropped
down dead on Monday afternoon in the Drill-
hall of the 14th Middlesex Rifles, Highgate, of
which corps he was a private. He had been
selected as one of the tiring party at the
funeral of Mr. Benwell, who belonged to the
same corps, and who was buried during the
afternoon with military honours.

Augustus Elliot, the young man who shot
himself and his paramour, Ellen Moore, at a
house in Hoxton, has appeared at the Wor-
ship-street Police-court for a formal hearing
of the charge against him. Ho was remanded.

An adjournment of the Bridget debate in
the Hungarian delegation has been occasioned
by the absence of the Ministers from the
sitting. They were required at a Council
held by the Emperor on his arrival at
Buda.

M. Thiers, in dining with the Prefect of the
Seine, has invited attention to the state of the
city finances, there being now a municipal
debt of 1,500,000,000 francs. Worse than
that, there is suspeoted to be equivocal
administration.

M. Barthelemy St. Hilaire has it in eon-
temptation to address a homily to the Deputy
for Savoy on the ultra. Republican manifesto
launched at Grenoble. It will forcibly present.
three objections to M. Gambetta's procedure—
that it brings the Republic again into question,
that it ignores the President's servieeeto the
Republic, and that it is hard on the bour-
geoisie.

Monsignor Dupanloup has set down his
crozier firmly on M. Jules Si1:13011'S latest
educational circular. His reverence counsels
the superiors of seminaries in his diocese to
take no notice of the document, as all reason-
able reforms that can be expected from them
have been anticipated.

A great religious manifestation took place
on Sunday last at Lourdes, France. As many
as three hundred and fifteen banners were
carried in procession to the Grotto of Notre
Dame de Lourdes, meat of them being very
tastefully worked and painted. All houses on
the route were decorated with wreathe of ever-
greens and flowers, white and blue hugs
being exhibited from many windows. When the
banners of Alsaoe and Lorraine came in sight
a good deal of enthusiasm was displayed, and
some of the peasants knelt and prayed for
their countrymen of the lost provinces. When,
too, the Archbishop of Auoh, in the dosing
sermon, alluded to the sufferings of Alsace and
Lorraine, few of his hearers could repress
their tears.

The barque Amelia, 700 tons, was towed
into Plymouth on Tuesday evening, having
been in collision on Monday with two vessels.
The Ameliu, about nine o'clook, ran into a
brig unknown, which, it is feared, sank, as
she must have been very seriously damaged.
Nothing was seen or heard of the crew. Two
hours afterwards the Amelia, whieh had
already received great dacaage about her bow,
was run into by a German ship, which cut her
down to the water's edge. This vessel will
be identified, as one of the Amelia's crew
scrambled on board her.

On Tuesday morning a man nained David
Miller, aged 72 years, was killed at the
Brighton Railway Station. Uiller, who had
been in the employment of the company for
about twenty-five years, was crossing the rails
from the sawing shed of the railway workshop&
with some planking on his shoulder. He
was thus unable to see an engine and tender
which were running into the station, and
which caught him, knocked him down, and
went over him. The injuries he sustained
were so great that he died soon afterwards.

On Saturday a testimonial was piesented to
Mr. Henry Fisher, assistant manager of the
Metropolitan Railway, that gentleman being
about to retire from the service, with which he
has been connected since the opening of the
line in 1803. In a very short space of time a
sum of about £l2O was subscribed by the
clerks, inspectors, guards, and other employes
of the company. The testimonial consisted of
a gold watch and chain, diamond ring, dress-
ing case, some handsome jewellery for Mrs.
Fisher, and an illuminated address on vellum,

At its final meeting at
.the Guildhall, the
Thames Shipping Inspection Committee en-
dorsed all the arrangements that had been
entered into with the Admiralty awl the Privy
Council for providing a cholera hospital on the
river, and ensuring the immediate isolation of
any ease of infection which might be imported.

Lambeth will shortly become too hot for
roughs. Two choice specimens, whom the
pollee described as a "terror to Peckham,"
have been fined £3, with the alternative of a
month's imprisonment, for refusing to leave
the Waterloo Arms on being refused drink.
They were also condemned injjs. for broken
glass and furniture, and had. to find bail for
three months.

Sir John Pakington on Monday evening
distributed tha prizes at the Leeds School of
Arts, and in doing so enlarged on the benefits
of mechanics' institutes, which, he affirmed,
were still in the hands of those for whom they
were designed, and had not been appropriated
by other classes. He dwelt emphatically on
the value of technical education.

In view of the serious importance which
is being attached to the next meeting of the
Permantnt Commission, efforts are being
made by the semi-official journals to quiet
public expectation. The Journal des Debuts
dissuades those Deputies who had announced
their intention to attend the meeting to recon-
sider their resolve, as their presence is
,not indispensable.

In opening the ltigsdag, the King of Den-
mark has made a symptomatic allusion to the
Schleswig question. He stated that it was still
pending, but added that he preserved the firm
hope of a satisfactory solution. The Czaro-
witeh, who was present, may have seen farther
into the riddle than most of the Deputies, but
the latter were highly gratified by what little
they could understand of it. They applauded
the Royal announcement heartily.

Frontier reprisals are about to commence
between France and Germany. M. de
Remnant has received notice from the German
Ambassador that after the Ist November pass-
ports properly vised at the German Consulate
will be required from all Frenchmen entering
Alsace-Loraine. The same practice is already
in force on the French side.

A deputation of licensed victuallers had an
interview with the Attorney-General at Exeter
on Wednesday on the subject of the Licensing
Act. The learned gentleman, it is stated, ad-
mitted that some of the provisions of the
measure were bad, and required amendment.

Telegraphic intelligence has been received
that the steamer George Cairns, while on a
voyage from Montreal to Liverpool, capsized
off Sydney, Cape Breton; that eight of her
crew were drowned, but the rest escaped in
boats.

The body Of Fanny Ann Everley, a girl 13
years of age, was found in the Surrey Canal,
Camberwell, on Wednesday morning. It is
supposed she had committed suicide.

A disastrous explosion occurred on Monday
afternoon at the extensive colliery of Messrs.
Ackroyd Brothers situated at Morley, a small

• AND PAINTERS.

On SAturday evening, a delegate meeting of the
above trades was held at the Bell Inn, Old Bailey,
relative to an advance of 10 per cent. on piece-
work, and fifty-four hours for a week's work.
Mr. Gaywood occupied the chair.
The Chairman said he was very glad to see so
many prescni, and that they had been so far suc-
cessful. Ile felt that everyone bad an important
duty to perform in assisting him. He heard that
,a member of the trade had been discharged for
supporting the movement, and he much regretted
this, but be was certain the trade would support
him. The committee has worked most cheerfully,
and there has not been the least ill-feeling. This
Is a meeting of delegates whose duty is to appoint
.officers for carrying out the movement.

Mr. Claywood was elected chairman; Mr.
Ruler, secretary; Mr. Dwight, tre isurer, and
Messrs. Pays, Tompkins, and Bristo, trustees.
Mr. Rider stated that tilt re was a balance in
hand of £l7 4s. 7d., and said that the time is fast
coming for nine hours a day. It is specified in
the press that they meant to abolish piece work.
This he denied. The movement is for 10 per
cent. advance on piece work for society men as
well as non-society men and labourers. Some said
they were rising for strikes, but let masters grant
reasonable requaits and this will put an end to
strikes. They did not wish to intimidate masters,
nor masters to intimidate men.

It was rose ved and carried, that a delegate
from each she should form a central committee
to assist the general provincial committee.
A delegate from Woolwich Arsenal said there
were 170 men in their shop. They expected a
rise of wages, and had been offered 6 per cent.
Some men had only 3d. per hour. If they were
not amalgamated capital could do what they liked,
but if they were united it would be different.
They wanted the men in London to work hand
and band with them.

The Chairman said they were quite welcome,
and he could say no more. lie was pleased the
delegate had attended, and if anything took place
in Woolwich tloy would try to prevent any of
their men going there.

It was resolved and carried that each member
should pay Bd. per week to ealry on the move-
ment.

After a rote of thanks to the press and chairman
proceedings were closed.

articles.title: ROPE AND TWINE SPINNERS.
articles.text:
THE ROPE AND TWINE SPINNERS.

The rope and twine spinners of Dundee, after
due consideration of their position and the stale of
trade, determined to solfct their employers for the
adoption of the fifty-one hours, which nearly
every trade and branch of industry in Dundee arc
bOvr enjoying. The employers refused to meet
them, and rejected every proposal which tended to
a peaceful settlement of the dispute. The men
saw • only one course left them, namely, to
strike. They did so on the 7th of last month, and
are still out, with the same determination as when
they first left the employers. Since the men left
work the masters have leagued themselves together
to stand against the men, and have imposed a £lO
flne on the first one who should give way, and
have forwarded the names of every man to each of
the employers in our trade in Scotland, with a
request that they should not employ them. Now,
the men have been workings 7 hours for 215., and
spinning 5,000 fathoms of rope yarn per day for
the ar. 6d., and twelve threads single and nine
double-handed, sixty-six yards per hour. The
concession of the employers to the Si hours would
only give them 5& per hour, a dock labourer's pay
in London, and these men mechanics seven years.
Tradesmen only asking ad. per hour are made to
strike for it. Can anyone call this unjust on the
part of' the men P And yet they are reported all
over Scotlawl, and are stigmatized by the em-
ployers for daring to ask a dock labourer's price.
The step taken by the employers has only inten-
sified the struggle, and will not be given up by
the men until they get their request.

Statesmen may counsel to moderation and the
press may condemn for striking, but employers
may get abundantly rich, and then refuse the
most moderato request of shortening the hours of
labour to 61 per wok, to receive ad. per hour.

Daniel Guile, in the monthly report, says
are glad to be able to say trade continues very
good; yet, from the tone of the report on the state
of trode, it is very evident there are signs of
decline, but not bf such a character as to excite
any alarm, for we niubt expect, as winter draws
.righ that there will be a curtailing of expenses in

many of the lArge engineering firms ;nor can this
be wondered at When we contemplate for a single
moment the exqrbitant price put on the rail
material by the large coal and ironmasters. They
are the men who by their unnatural desire for
gain are doing all they can to drive the trade from
the country, and they have the audacity to try to
blind the public by. laying the blame upon the
advance in wages and shortening of the hours of
labour, while at the same time they know thztt for
every polity the working miner has received,
either by the advance, or the shortening of his
working hours, they themselves have received
above a shilling. But let both us and our imme-
diate- employers be patient; this delusion must
soon pass away, and like all other false theories,
will soon come to an end.

It may not be out of place to give the thoughts
of our brethren in the United States of America on
this subject, as taken from their monthly journal
for August, as it will show that we are not alone
In our views on this subject. The ure as
follows :

We are pleased to note the continued good times
in the foundry business. Trade everywhere
seems to be rushing, especially in the stove. branch.
:Ilealora are in demand, and everything points to
a prosperous fall trade, the continued scarcity and
high price of iron being • the only drawback,
although the scarcity has not, so fur as we can
learn, affected anything but prices for the raw and
manufactured article; no foundries or rolling mills
are closed for want of iron, and we doubt nut that
the supply will be arnplo at present prices. Ex-
perience has taught us that the presqrit ru-li will
nut last very long, and we urge npon our members
to prepare for the reaction, whether it be natural
or forced. While we have reason to believe that
until Christmai work will be steady, yet beyond
that date no one can speak with any certainty.
It therefore becomes us, profiting by past experi-
ence, to prepare for dull times—, in time of peace
prepare tor war;' perfect your Union; get its
treasury in good condition; square your individual
accounts with the Unioit ; and, above all, look to
your own individual treasury. A word to the
&c.
We can only re-echo the advice given in the
American Journal, and say that in all probability
trade may continue goad until the end of the year;
after that, we may consider belongs more especially
to the future, and we are, to some extent, pre-
pared for it, having Jaid on one side a pretty
tolerable amount of cash, so that we shall not be
entirely powerless should the worst results of the
market riggers be brought about, our cash in
hand already amounting to over £34,000. But
let us not be weary in well-doing, but rather let
us watch and be careful; and though we may not
be able to hinder that over which we have no
control, yet we shall at least be able to break to
801110 extent the force of the coming storm. To
be forewarned is to be forearmed.

THE WIGAN TRADES COUNCIL
AND BOARDS OF ARBITRA.
TION.

On Tuesday', a meeting of the Wigan Trades
Council was held at the Raven Hotel, Wallgate.
Mr. Almond in the chair.

The Chairman explained that they were espe-
cially met together to discuss the question of
arbitration.

Mr. R. Cornish, the secretary, introduced the
subject by reading a paper, which fully explained
the principles upon which arbitration should be
conducted. lie earnestly recommended the whole
subject to the attention of the trades of Wigan.
Mr. Parker moved, and Mr. Smith seconded the
follcwing resolution, which was carried with only
two dissentients :--

That in the opinion of this council the only wise
and rational way of settling trade disputes, is by
the system of arbitration and conciliation, and
this council pledges itself to use every endeavour
to get the principle practically adopted in Wigan.
The committee was then empowered to take
steps to carry the resolution into effect.
A vote of thanks to Mr. Cornish for his paper
brought the proceedings to a close.

articles.text:
THE LONDON BAKERS.

On 'Wednesday evening there was a crowded
attendance at the meeting of the London Council
of Operative Bakers at the committee-rooms,
Admiral Carter, Bartholornew-closo. Mr. Cook-
man stated, on behalf of the strike committee, that
the persons who were reaping the benefit of the
movement were the master bakers, and not the
journeymen. The reports they had received were
not of a very encouraging character, as they were
mostly to the effect that both the masters and men
were fast returuing to the old system. In conse-
quence of this a communication had been for-
warded to the Master Bakers"frade Protection
Society asking them to meet the men's delegation
again, but he was sorry to inform them that no
answer had been received. If the masters would
not meet them again in conference, he contended

that nothir4 Was gaiiied: by the movement. The
,Chairman eaid when the strike committee was
elected they were vested with full pOwer, and he
thought they had not, exceeded their duty. Sub-
sequently Mr. Webb proposed, and Mr. Evershed
seconded :7--

That the functions of the strike committee
having now ceased, the bakers trade council beg to
withdraw the latter.

Mr. Cockman said the moticn was equivalent to
passing a vote of censure on the committee. In
the discussion which ensued various opinions of
an adverse character were expressed. It was
understood that no more levies were to be
received, but that each branch was to support its
own out-of-place men. After a long and compli-
cated discussion, it was understood that the strike
was at an end, and that the future action should
be taken into consideration at the next meeting of
the council.

L The Congress shall consist only of delegates
representing bona fide Trades Societies, and
Trades Councils, and similar bodies, by whatever
name they may, for the time being, be called.
Each delegate shall come provided with a
credential signed by the officers of the society or
council he represents, csrtifying to his appoint-
ment, such credential to he given up to the floor°.
tury, immediately on his arrival at the Con-
grass.
3. The time of meeting shall be as follows
on the first day to assemble at 12 o'clock noon
'prompt ; on all other days at 9 30 a.m. ; adjourn
at 1. re-assemble at 2, and adjourn at 5 o'elook
• each day.
4. The roll shall be called promptly to time
morning and afternoon, the names of all dele-
gates late or absent to be read over with the
minutes each morning.
6. At tie opening of the annual Congress, the
Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee shall
take the chair pro forma until the Congress has
elected its own President.
6. A committee of three shall be elected to
examine the credentials, und report thereon to the
meeting.
7. The delegates shall then proceed to elect the
President of the Congress, preference being given
to a delegate_of the town where .the Congress is
being .
,
8. The Congress shall then elect a Seeratary-,'a
like preference being given. .
9. The Congress shall then elect a vice-Presi-
dent, adoor.keeper and a messenger.
10. A standing committee of five shall then be
elected, to whom shall be remitted the whole
business of the Congress; the order of and subjects
for discussion, together with the whole financial
arrangements of the Congress. :The vide-president
to be the chairman of the committee.
11. After the routine business of election or
:officers snd committee, the president shall formally
open the CongreA with an addiesa.
12. The standing committee, with a view to
securing a proper despatch of bueiness, with perfect.
faireess to ali who have been to the trouble to
preplire papers, of which due notice bas been,
give", halL have power to divide the Congress
into sections, so thar. those specially interested in
any particular question may have the fullest
opportunity for its discussion. -
1 S. The standing otnamittet shall be allowed to

retire at 4 o'clock each dtflone hour
closing the sittings of Congress), for the purpose
of selecting and arroving the next dm s pro-
gramtne.

14. Each delegate shall pay to the "treasurer, on
the first day of his arrival, the sum of 10s. towards

repreFoinalitere than oho society, 103..4
for every
such society he is delegated to represent The.
names of those ;who have, and those who have not

following learning. No person shall be deemed a
member of Congress until his 100 is paid.
• 16. The reader of a paper shall be allowed
twenty minutes; the mover of a resolution fifteen
minutes; succeeding speakers ten minutes each;
no one shall speak more than once on any one
question. After the reply, no one shall be allowed
to speak on the question before the chair, but it
shall be at once put to the vote by the chairman.
16. No second amendment, or rider to an ori-
ginal proposition, shall be put to the vote until
the first amendment is disposed of.
17. The voting shall be by show of hands; but
in ease of a dispute, the chairman may oieler a
division.
18. Two tellers shall be appointed by the Con-
gress, and their ruling shill be final. . .
19. If more than one amendment is proposed,
the standing committee may retire, together with
the movers of the resolution and amendments, for
the purpose of trying to secure unanimity, by
blending the amendments in such a manner as will
be Most conducive to the harmony of Congress
and the despatch of business.
' 20. No delegate shall be allowed to read a
second paper until after all other papers' of which
notice has been previously given, have been read,
unless by special permission and sanction of the
standing committee, and the formal consent of
Congress.
21. In the selection of papers to be read, pre-
ference shall be given to those of which notice has
been given, and in the order in which they have
been received by the committee.
22. Subjects having special reference to the
trade of the town or locality where the Ct;ngress
is being held, shall in no case be allowed to oc-
cupy the time ef more than one sitting of the
congress. And it is desirable that .these special
subjects be laid before the committee as early as
practicable, for the purpose of arranging them
under one or two general heads, and emoodying
them in one or two simple propositions.
23. No dele.cate shall leave- the ro an without
the consent of the Vice-President: and delegates
absent one whole sitting without leave of absence,
shall be named by the Chairman.
24. A General or Parliamentary Committee of
nine shall be elected on the last day of eon Con-
grass, who shall continue in office until they
are re-elected, or their successors are appointed.

President, Treasurer, and Secretary for the
ensuing year; and they also shall remain in
office until they are re-elected, or their successors

expenses of the Congress, :hall be handed over to
the Treasurer of the Parliamentary Committee for
the general purposes of such Committee.
26. The duties of the Parliamentary Com-
mittee shall be (1) to watch all legislative
measures directly affecting the questions of labour,
and (2) to initiate, whenever necessary, such
legislative action as Congress may direct, or as the
exigencies of the time and circumstances may.
demand.

committee, shall have authority to solicit sub-
scriptions, donations, or levies, for the purpose of
defraying the expenses incurred by such com-
mittee; but the mode of payment shall be left
optional with each society as to whether it shall
pay by levy or donation.

by the President,tafter the maul routine business

mentary Secretary, and shall lay it on the table

and co-operate with the local committee of the
town where the next Congress is to be held, for
the purpose of making the arrangements as com-
plete as possible and preparing the questions to
be discus,ed, and together to take such Joint action
as the business or other special circumstances of
the time may render necessary or desirable.

to invite persons to attend the sittings of the Con-
gress whose presence they may deem advisable
